title: Support operations: knowledge, escalation and metrics
summary: Capturing knowledge as you solve tickets, handing work off cleanly, and the six support metrics a manager will ask about.

lessons.title: Knowledge-centered service
lessons.body:
**Knowledge-Centered Service (KCS)** is a method from the Consortium for Service Innovation. Its idea: write and improve knowledge articles as part of solving tickets, not as a separate project afterward. The Consortium's v6 Practices Guide is free online. You do not need certification to use the habits.

KCS describes a loop, often summarised as **capture, structure, reuse, improve**:

1. **Search first.** Before answering, search the knowledge base for the customer's words. If an article exists, **link it** to the ticket and use it. That link is a record of reuse.
2. **Fix if wrong.** If the article is outdated, unclear or missing a step, correct it right then. Do not leave a note for later.
3. **Create if absent.** If nothing exists, write a short article from the ticket while the details are fresh.
4. **Publish at the right visibility.** Some articles are internal drafts for agents, and some are verified for customers.

**An article that works** has the customer's wording as the title, one problem per article, and a structure like this:

```text
Title: Shift start time shows an hour off for Arizona pharmacists
Problem: A shift for an Arizona pharmacist shows one hour earlier or later than expected.
Environment: Web and mobile app, version 2.3.x
Cause: Arizona does not observe daylight saving time (fixed in 2.3.3)
Resolution: 1. Open the shift. 2. Check the pharmacist's profile time zone is America/Phoenix...
Related: Ticket DISP-401, article 'Change a shift start time'
Owner: Support. Reviewed: 2026-11-01
```

**What to measure.** Link rate (share of tickets with an article attached), reuse count per article, and deflection (customers who read an article and did not file a ticket). Old articles need an owner and a review date, or they mislead.

**Your own case.** Rewriting end-user documentation and the knowledge base cut ticket inflow by 35% in your last role. The tickets.csv practice data shows the same shape: 'How do I' tickets run about 38 a month from January to April and fall to about 11 a month from May. KCS is the habit that keeps that gain: every repeated question becomes an article, and every article gets used.

Common failures: articles written in internal jargon, no review date, ten articles covering the same question, and agents who copy answers into tickets instead of linking.
keyPoints: Search the knowledge base first and link the article you use.
Fix a wrong article when you find it; create one when none exists.
Write the title in the customer's words, one problem per article.
Articles need an owner and a review date.
lessons.interviewAngle: This is your strongest ticket-process story. Tell it with numbers: what questions repeated, what you wrote, how you checked the 35% drop and over which months. Do not claim formal KCS certification unless you have it; say you applied the same habit of writing articles from tickets.

exercises.prompt: In KCS, what should an agent do first when a new ticket arrives?
choices: Search the knowledge base for the customer's wording and reuse or fix an article
exercises.explanation: Search first, then link to an existing article, correct it, or create a new one if none exists.

exercises.prompt: Which is the best article title?
choices: Shift start time shows an hour off for Arizona pharmacists
exercises.explanation: Customers search in their own words, and a clear title says the symptom.

exercises.prompt: Using the fact that 'How do I export the monthly assignments' was filed 47 times in the practice tickets, write the knowledge base article that would reduce it. Include title, steps and where you would link it.
exercises.answer:
**Title:** How do I export the monthly assignments?
**Applies to:** Dispatcher and admin roles, web app.
**Steps:** 1. Open Reports > Assignments. 2. Choose the month. 3. Select Export and choose CSV. 4. Open the downloaded file in Excel.
**If the export is empty:** check the month and that you have the Admin role.
**Related:** 'Where do I see who accepted a request'.
**Owner:** Support. Review date: three months out.
**Link it:** in the portal's suggested articles, in the product's Export button help text, and in any ticket reply that asks about export.
rubric: Places to link it for deflection

lessons.title: Escalation paths and handoffs
lessons.body:
Support is usually tiered. A common structure:

| Tier | Does | Hands off when |
|---|---|---|
| **Tier 1** (front line) | Logs, categorises, answers from the knowledge base, resets access | A fix needs product knowledge, data access or investigation |
| **Tier 2** | Reproduces, checks data and logs, workarounds | A code change or a system fault is needed |
| **Tier 3** (engineering) | Diagnoses and fixes code and infrastructure | |

Two kinds of escalation exist. **Functional** escalation moves the ticket to a more specialised group. **Hierarchical** escalation brings in management because of impact, customer importance or a missed target. Mixing them up confuses people.

**Escalate when:** the SLA will breach, the severity is Critical or High, a customer asks, the issue is out of your permission, or you have no next step. **Do not** escalate to avoid reading the ticket.

**A handoff note that works** answers the next person's first five questions so they do not call the customer again:

```text
Summary: Arizona pharmacists' shifts display one hour off in the app
Customer: Mesa Care Pharmacy (id 12), contact Dana; impact: 6 shifts this week
What I did: reproduced on web and iOS; checked pharmacist time zone (America/Phoenix)
Evidence: screenshots, shift ids 8812, 8815; steps in ticket
Why escalating: needs a code change; severity Major
Customer has been told: investigating, next update Friday 10:00
Workaround: check times in dispatcher view
Ask: please confirm cause and fix version
```

**Rules.** Keep the ticket owner visible: when you hand off, say who now owns it. Stay the customer's contact unless the customer is told otherwise. Never 'throw over the wall' with the bare words 'please look'. Record the handoff time, since it feeds metrics such as time in each tier.

**Bounce risk.** A ticket that moves between groups three times usually has a missing routing rule or a missing owner. Fix the rule, not the ticket.

When you receive a bad handoff, ask specific questions once, on the ticket, and improve the template so it does not repeat.
keyPoints: Tiers hand work upward; functional escalation changes the group, hierarchical adds management.
Escalate on SLA risk, high severity, missing permission or no next step.
A handoff note must hold impact, evidence, what was tried and what the customer was told.
Name the owner after every handoff.
lessons.interviewAngle: You were the liaison between customers and developers, which is escalation in daily practice. Give one example of a handoff note you wrote that stopped a developer needing to call the customer. Add that you update the handoff template when a receiver has to ask the same question twice.

exercises.prompt: A manager is brought in because a key customer is unhappy about a missed deadline. This is:
exercises.explanation: Bringing in management for impact or a missed target is hierarchical escalation. Moving to a specialist group is functional.

choices: Customer says app is wrong. Escalating.
Arizona shifts display 1h off on web and iOS; reproduced; shift ids 8812, 8815; customer told update Fri 10:00; need cause and fix version.
exercises.explanation: It gives impact, evidence, what was done, what the customer knows and the ask.

exercises.prompt: Write the handoff note for this: Tier 1 has a ticket where pharmacists at one pharmacy are not receiving emergency alerts. You confirmed their phone numbers are correct and that other pharmacies receive alerts. Fill any gaps with plausible details.
exercises.answer:
**Summary:** Pharmacists at Riverside Pharmacy (id 22) are not receiving emergency shift alerts; other pharmacies are.
**Impact:** Two emergency shifts went unfilled this week; Major severity.
**Checked:** phone numbers valid; notification setting enabled; alerts reach pharmacists at other pharmacies.
**Evidence:** shift ids 9021 and 9034, no alert log entries for them.
**Customer told:** we are investigating and will update by 15:00 tomorrow; fill urgent shifts by phone with support.
**Ask:** check the alert service logs and distance data for pharmacy 22; confirm cause.
**Owner after handoff:** Tier 2, I remain the customer contact.
rubric: States what the customer was told

lessons.title: Support metrics: first response, resolution, reopen, backlog age, deflection and CSAT
lessons.body:
Zendesk, Atlassian and ITIL material define the same few measures. Definitions vary a little by tool, so state your definition when you quote a number.

| Metric | Definition | Watch for |
|---|---|---|
| **First response time** | Creation to the first useful public reply | Zendesk counts only a public reply, so an automatic 'received' message that stops the clock can hide slow human replies |
| **Time to resolution** | Creation to resolved | Report the median and the long tail, not only the average |
| **Reopen rate** | Share of resolved tickets that reopen | High means weak fixes or weak verification |
| **Backlog age** | Age of open tickets, in buckets (0-2d, 3-7d, 8-30d, 30d+) | A few very old tickets hide in a healthy average |
| **Deflection** | Customers who read an article and did not file a ticket | Hard to measure exactly; track article views against ticket volume |
| **CSAT** | Share of 'good' ratings among survey responses (good divided by total, times 100) | Few responses, so show the count |

Add two more: **Requester wait time** (time the customer waits on you, excluding time when you waited for them) and **volume by category** (what people ask about).

**Worked example with the practice data** (734 tickets, Jan to early Oct 2026):

- Category mix: 205 How do I, 184 Bug, 123 Access, 122 Feature request, 100 Data fix.
- Average open-to-close time by severity: critical about 2.4 hours, high 7.5, medium 20.6, low 37.9. The ordering matches the severity.
- Nine tickets are still open at the end of the data.
- 'How do I' tickets: about 151 in January to April versus about 54 in May to September.

You can read this as: resolution speed follows severity as it should; self-serve content moved volume.

**Gaming and traps.** First response time can be gamed with auto-replies, and resolution time by closing tickets early. A rising reopen rate is the signal. CSAT is skewed by who answers surveys. Pair a speed metric with a quality metric, for example first response with CSAT.

**Cadence.** Review weekly: volume, backlog age, SLA met, reopens, top five topics. Ask what to change, not who to blame.
keyPoints: State your definition when quoting first response or resolution time.
Use median and buckets, not only averages.
Pair speed metrics with quality metrics such as reopen rate and CSAT.
Volume by category shows what knowledge or product fixes would remove work.
lessons.interviewAngle: Quote your 35% inflow reduction with the period and the method. Say you used SQL to count tickets by category and month. Do not invent first response or CSAT numbers you never measured. If you cite a percentage, say what two periods you compared and how you counted, so it survives a follow-up question.

exercises.prompt: Fifty tickets were resolved this month and 5 were reopened. What is the reopen rate?
Why might 'average time to resolution' mislead?
choices: A few very long tickets pull it up and hide the typical case, so show the median and the long tail
exercises.explanation: Skewed data makes the mean a poor summary. The median and age buckets tell the real story.

exercises.prompt: In the practice data, which category has the most tickets?
exercises.explanation: There are 205 'How do I' tickets, more than the 184 bugs.

exercises.prompt: Your manager asks for a one-paragraph weekly support summary and gives you these numbers: 62 new tickets, 58 resolved, median first response 3h, median resolution 19h, 6 reopened, 11 tickets older than 30 days, CSAT 92% from 12 responses. Write the summary and name one concern.
exercises.answer: This week we received 62 tickets and resolved 58, so the backlog grew by 4. Median first response was 3 hours and median resolution 19 hours. Six of the resolved tickets reopened (about 10%), which is the number I would watch: fixes or verification may be weak. Eleven tickets are older than 30 days and need an owner or a decision. CSAT was 92%, but from only 12 responses, so I would not lean on it. Concern: the reopen rate and the ageing tickets, which I will review by category next week.
rubric: Computes reopen rate from the data
Names a concern and a next step
